_meta.description: The change backlog for this site, written so a reviewer can choose a path before anything is implemented. Every suggestion states what it changes, why it is worth doing, what it costs, what it risks, how it can be checked, whether any official rule constrains it, and what evidence would show it worked. Nothing here is implemented: the register is a decision surface, not a changelog.

priorities.P1 - Decide first: A decision here changes what other suggestions are even possible, or the item blocks the site from doing its job.
priorities.P2 - Adds real value: The site works without it; adding it materially improves reader trust, usefulness or search eligibility.
priorities.P3 - Housekeeping: Accuracy or consistency of the records themselves. Low risk, no reader-visible gain.

suggestions.title: Apply for Creators API access so prices and ratings can be published lawfully
suggestions.problem: Prices, star ratings and review counts are deliberately blank across the site because the Associates Participation Requirements allow them only when Amazon serves the link or the data comes from an approved Amazon API (Section 2(b) and 6(t)). Twelve of the site's twenty-one pages therefore tell a reader less than the product page does. Flag F-02.
suggestions.proposal: Enrol in Amazon Associates, reach the qualifying-sales prerequisite Amazon states for API registration, register for the Creators API through Associates Central, and feed a cached, timestamped price and rating through the build. Until that exists, keep the cells blank exactly as they are now.
suggestions.why: A buying guide without a price or a rating is a specification sheet. Readers comparing three air fryers will leave for a page that answers the obvious question, and search engines have little reason to prefer this page over the listing itself. Adding price and rating is the single largest reader-value gain available.
suggestions.effort: Prerequisite sales volume is the real cost and it cannot be shortcut; registration itself is an administrative step. The build change is small: one cached field per product plus the existing disclosure.
suggestions.risk: Amazon's own documentation states the API is only for the marketplace registered and requires prior written approval for certain reuse. A stale cached price shown as current would be a consumer-protection problem as well as a policy one, so the timestamp must be visible.
suggestions.check: A published price carries a visible observation timestamp and reconciles with the value the API returned in the same run; any product without a fresh value shows blank, not an old number.

suggestions.title: Say plainly who writes the site, and how the content is produced
suggestions.problem: No page states who is responsible for the content, and the articles read as machine output: identical structure, identical sentence rhythm, the same hedged qualifier in every piece. Google's guidance on people-first content asks who created a page, how it was created, and why, and treats unmanaged generative output as low effort; it also warns that fabricated author identities are a deception signal. The honest answer here is 'a research pipeline, reviewed by the site owner', and that is publishable.
suggestions.proposal: Add a short editorial note, repeated in the article footer: what the pipeline collects, what a human reviews before publishing, the date of the last review, and a contact route. Do not invent an author name, headshot or credential. If the owner is willing to be named as the reviewer, name them; if not, describe the review process without inventing a person.
suggestions.why: This is the difference between a site a reader trusts and one that reads as bulk output, and it is what the 'does not read like AI slop' request is actually about. It also converts an unavoidable fact, automation, into a stated method rather than something a reader has to guess.
suggestions.effort: One data field, one template block, one rebuild. Under an hour.
suggestions.risk: A vague or boilerplate editorial note is worse than none. It has to name a real review step; if no human reviews the copy, the note must say so.
suggestions.check: Every article page shows the note; the note names a review step that actually happened on the stated date; no invented person appears anywhere on the site.

sources.ref: Who / How / Why; effort and originality; fabricated authorship warning

suggestions.title: Give every page its own title and meta description
suggestions.problem: Sixteen of the twenty-one pages share one identical meta description, so every page a search engine sees describes itself the same way. Google's snippet guidance asks for a unique description per page. The five article pages already do this correctly, which proves the template can.
suggestions.proposal: Write one meta description and one title per page from what the page actually contains, extending the field the article pages already use to every page in the builder.
suggestions.why: Duplicate descriptions make the site look like one repeated page to a crawler and give a reader no reason to pick one result over another. It is the cheapest visible improvement available and it touches nothing that needs a policy review.
suggestions.effort: Fifteen short texts plus a small builder change. Two to three hours including review.
suggestions.risk: Descriptions must not promise what the page withholds; a description that implies a price when the price is blank is a new accuracy defect.
suggestions.check: The build fails if any two pages share a meta description, and each description is checked against the page's own headings.

sources.ref: Create unique descriptions for each page on your site

suggestions.title: Mark the affiliate links rel="sponsored" without breaking the required disclosure
suggestions.problem: Outbound product links carry rel="noopener noreferrer" only. Google's link-qualification guidance says paid links should be qualified with rel="sponsored" (or nofollow), and its spam policy treats undisclosed payment-for-links arrangements as link spam. Amazon separately requires the visible disclosure, which no attribute can replace.
suggestions.proposal: Add rel="sponsored" alongside the existing rel values on the three product calls to action, and keep both the adjacent '(paid link)' label and the Operating Agreement sentence exactly where they are.
suggestions.why: It costs one attribute and removes a plausible reading of the outbound links as unqualified paid links. It does not change what a reader sees, so it cannot cost conversions.
suggestions.effort: One template change, one rebuild.
suggestions.risk: None identified for the reader. The temptation to treat the attribute as a substitute for the disclosure must be resisted; the guidance is explicit that qualification does not replace a visible disclosure, and Amazon's rule does not accept an attribute in place of the sentence.
suggestions.check: Every outbound product link carries rel="sponsored" and still sits next to a paid-link label and the disclosure sentence; the QA audit fails if either the attribute or the disclosure goes missing.

suggestions.title: Add the one thing a listing cannot tell a reader: what the appliance is like to live with
suggestions.problem: Every article is a restatement of the specification table. No page records noise, how a basket actually cleans, how long a preheat takes, or whether the footprint fits under a cabinet. A reader can get the specification table from the listing in one click, so the site currently adds nothing over the source it cites.
suggestions.proposal: Do not invent experience. Either (a) buy, borrow or borrow-time with one unit per format and record dated, first-person notes with photographs, or (b) keep the site explicitly positioned as a specification and decision-tool site, state that no unit was tested, and drop the review vocabulary that implies otherwise.
suggestions.why: This is the substance behind Google's thin-affiliation policy, which names rigorous testing and original reviews as what separates a good affiliate page from a copied one. It is also the only sustainable reason a reader would choose this page over the listing.
suggestions.effort: (a) is weeks and has a real cash cost. (b) is a copy edit and a positioning decision.
suggestions.risk: (a) creates a conflict-of-interest question that must be disclosed: a unit supplied free by a seller cannot be presented as an independent purchase. (b) gives up any claim to be a review site.
suggestions.check: Either every testing claim is backed by a dated note and a photograph taken by the site, or the site states in one visible sentence that no unit was tested and no page uses the word 'review' to describe its own content.

sources.ref: Thin affiliation: good affiliate pages offer meaningful content such as original reviews, rigorous testing, navigation and comparisons

Disclosure obligations when a relationship exists with a seller

suggestions.title: Answer the questions people actually type, one page per question
suggestions.problem: The five published articles target product nouns ('dual basket air fryer', '8 quart air fryer'). They do not answer the format-choice questions a buyer types before they know which product they want, and no page addresses the two inconsistencies the research found (capacity units, the P2 function count) as a standalone answer.
suggestions.proposal: Publish a small set of decision-first pages built from the same verified fact tables: 'dual basket or single basket for a family of four', '6 quart versus 6 litre: why the numbers differ', 'air fryer footprint versus counter depth', and 'what 24 versus 25 cooking functions means on one listing'. Each answers one question and links to the three product records as the worked example.
suggestions.why: Format questions arrive before brand questions, so they are winnable earlier for a new site, and they are answerable entirely from facts already verified here. They also give the site a reason to exist beyond three product pages, which is what both the thin-affiliation and scaled-content policies look for.
suggestions.effort: Half a day per page including verification, because the facts already exist.
suggestions.risk: Volume without value trips the scaled-content policy. The guard is that each page must answer a different question; if two pages would say the same thing, they must be one page.
suggestions.check: No two question pages share a thesis; every claim on each page resolves to an existing sourced fact row; the number of pages is driven by distinct questions, not by a target count.

suggestions.title: Replace the 4.50% category figure with the rate that actually applies to these ASINs
suggestions.problem: The site quotes Amazon's public Table 1 Kitchen rate of 4.50% while marking every product cell blank, because no official source maps a specific ASIN to a commission category (F-01). A reader gets a number that is real but not about them, and the site gets a number it cannot use.
suggestions.proposal: Read the assigned commission category for each ASIN in Associates Central (the account owner is the only party who can), record it against the product, and publish the per-ASIN rate with that assignment as its source. If the assignment cannot be read, delete the 4.50% quote entirely rather than leaving a figure that cannot be applied.
suggestions.why: Half-publishing a rate is worse than not publishing one: it invites a reader to multiply and gives them a wrong answer. Either the per-ASIN figure is sourced, or the whole commission discussion belongs on an internal analysis page rather than the landing page.
suggestions.effort: Minutes in Associates Central once the account exists; otherwise a copy deletion.
suggestions.risk: The assignment can change. A published rate needs the date it was read, in the same way a price would.
suggestions.check: Every published rate has a named category assignment, a read date and a source; if any is missing the cell is blank rather than defaulted.

suggestions.title: Decide the site's voice, and rewrite the articles to it once
suggestions.problem: The copy is accurate and unreadable. Every article opens by defining its own category, every paragraph ends with a hedging clause, and the same rhetorical shape repeats five times. Nothing on the site makes a recommendation, which is what a buyer came for. The cause is a writing rule that permits only restatement of verified fields; the effect is that the site answers nothing.
suggestions.proposal: Keep the fact rule and change the writing rule: allow the writer to conclude, rank within the verified facts, and address the reader directly, while every factual claim still resolves to a sourced row. Rewrite the five pieces to that standard and let the fact table carry the audit trail instead of the prose.
suggestions.why: This is the difference between the site as it reads now and a polished marketing site. A comparison page that refuses to compare is a table with sentences around it. Allowing judgement on top of verified facts adds originality without adding risk, and Google's guidance on helpful content rewards exactly that while treating pure restatement as low value.
suggestions.effort: Two days for five pieces plus review, most of it writing.
suggestions.risk: The moment the writer is allowed to conclude, the fact rule starts to slip. The guard has to be mechanical: a claim without a fact id fails the build, and a ranking claim must cite the field that supports it.
suggestions.check: Every paragraph still resolves to at least one fact row; each product article states who the product suits; the comparison page ranks the three formats on at least one listed attribute; no sentence asserts a fact that is not in a fact table.

sources.ref: Originality, insight beyond the obvious, and value to the reader

suggestions.title: Approve a format-first topic calendar: eight catchy, spec-backed articles
suggestions.problem: The brief asks for catchy, trendy articles and topics that can earn organic traffic, but the content program stops at five pieces and the register carries no topic plan. Without an approved list, each new article is invented ad hoc and the internal link structure that makes a small site findable never gets built.
suggestions.proposal: Adopt these eight working titles as the calendar, in two waves. Wave one, the foundational four: 'Air Fryer Sizes Explained: 6QT vs 8QT vs 26QT - What Actually Fits Your Counter'; 'Choosing an Air Fryer in 2026: The Format-First Method' (a rewrite of the published guide); 'Hi-Fry, Sync Finish, Shake Reminder: An Air Fryer Feature Glossary'; 'The First-Air-Fryer Checklist: Seven Numbers to Check Before You Buy'. Wave two: 'Two Baskets or One? The Sync-Finish Question, Answered With Specs'; 'French Door Air Fryer Ovens: Big Capacity, Bigger Footprint?'; 'Compact Countertop Cooking: The Small-Kitchen Air Fryer Format'; "What '24 Cooking Functions' Really Means (and Why Titles Disagree)". Every piece is written from the verified listing fields already in data/products.json and links to the format pages, so wave one needs no new verification.
suggestions.why: Format, size and feature questions are how people actually shop for air fryers, and each of these topics can be answered honestly from the sourced field set - catchy without a single unearned superlative. The four foundational pieces also build the link hub the five existing reviews need to become findable.
suggestions.effort: One article per working session once the voice decision (S-12) is recorded; wave one is four pieces.
suggestions.risk: Search demand is unmeasured (F-15): these are reasoned topic picks, not volume data. Writing before the voice decision risks a rewrite under S-12.
suggestions.check: Each published topic carries its own sourced fact table and links to at least two format pages; first-party Search Console data shows impressions for the topic cluster within a quarter.

It carries bracketed slots for the picks this queue is about to record: brand, visual direction, voice, topic wave. Fill the slots after D-17 to D-19 are recorded, then hand the prompt to a designer or a design tool. The Suggestions page also carries a shorter paste-ready brief from session arena/d8564cd0-zone4; D-20 decides which draft becomes the working brief.
suggestions.why: It turns the suggestions on this page into an executable brief, and it hard-codes the compliance rules so no visual idea can override them. Preparing it costs nothing; adopting it prevents a redesign that has to be re-done.

suggestions.risk: Freezing the brief before the picks would bake in placeholders; that is why adoption is sequenced after D-17 to D-19.

suggestions.title: Choose the visual direction and settle the brand name
suggestions.problem: The brief asks for a polished marketing affiliate website that does not read like machine output. The current look is compliant and legible but neutral, a warm identity refresh has since shipped as a no-decision-needed first step (session arena/d8564cd0-zone4) though the visual direction itself was never put to a decision, and the repository still carries two product names (F-39). The identity itself - name, tone of the hero, the shape of the first screen - is undecided, and external branding waits on it.
suggestions.proposal: Pick one direction: A. Warm editorial (kitchen-magazine): serif display, cream and terracotta, story-led hero - the stylesheet's theme layer is a light preview of this. B. Crisp data-journalism: keep the dashboard bones and sharpen the verified-facts framing into a trust-first publication. C. Bold deal-finder: high-contrast badges and urgency, though most of its price-led playbook is blocked by the price and rating rules (F-02). Settle the brand name in the same decision, and close F-39 with it.
suggestions.why: The look is the first thing the brief judges, and the name is the most expensive thing to change later. One decision here prevents a rename that resets every external signal the site earns.
suggestions.effort: The decision itself is an afternoon; the overhaul it authorises is scoped by DESIGN_PROMPT.md (S-14).
suggestions.risk: Choosing C would push against the withheld-price constraints; choosing a name without clearing it risks the trade-name problem in Q-19.
suggestions.check: One name appears in the repository, the site and the code (F-39 closed), and the first screen matches the chosen direction without losing the disclosure or the sourced-table discipline.

suggestions.title: Adopt a written evidence rule for 'trending' and popularity claims
suggestions.problem: The brief asks for trending-product analysis, but no trend or conversion signal is verified (F-15). The word 'trending' is exactly where marketing copy turns into unverifiable hype, and this project exists to prevent that.
suggestions.proposal: Write the rule into the publishing checklist: a popularity claim is allowed only as a dated snapshot of an official page - for example, a stated position on the official Air Fryers category ordering, read on a stated date - and never as a bare adjective. Later, first-party Search Console data may describe what readers read here, attributed to this site's own data and never to the market.
suggestions.why: It keeps the door open to genuinely trendy, engaging copy while every claim stays checkable against a dated official source.
suggestions.effort: One checklist entry and a sentence in the voice rule.

suggestions.title: No published surface may print a register count it does not read from the registers
suggestions.problem: The counts the site publishes about itself were the last prose that could silently age. ENGINE.md documented a test total the suite had outgrown and README's data-map row carried a flags numeral two flags behind its own enumeration (both live drift on main ed4f66a, flag F-94); and every parallel session this week has had to reconcile README and EXECUTIVE_SUMMARY numerals by hand after another session appended rows, because the two documents type the numbers as prose.
suggestions.proposal: Extend the recorded SG-37 mechanism from the two documents it names to every hand-typed surface: one checker (scripts/check_doc_counts.py) computes suggestions, questions, decisions (recorded and open), flags, requirements and the unittest discovery total from the registers and tests/; a Site-checks CI step and unit tests fail any disagreement; --fix rewrites numerals in place, never prose. The part that remains proposed: fold the same rule into scripts/verify.py so the gate runs wherever the build gates run (a logged request - verify.py sat inside arena/f598c2b6-zone4's open PR #103 claimed scope when the row was written; PR #103 merged while this session worked, so the request transfers to whoever owns verify.py next), and rely on the builder's existing computed counts for the generated pages (the Decision-centre meta description and the About-page governance line already read the registers at build time, so they cannot drift).
suggestions.why: A decision-support register that publishes wrong counts about itself undermines the same trust the register exists to protect. The gate turns count reconciliation from every session's chore into something a reintroduced stale numeral cannot survive: the CI step and the unit-test suite both fail before a drifted document can merge.
suggestions.effort: About two hours for the checker, CI step and tests (done 2026-11-19); under one hour to fold the rule into scripts/verify.py now that its claimed scope has freed.
suggestions.risk: Low. Rewrites are numerals-only by construction (the substitution keeps every non-captured character). When a document is intentionally reworded the gate fails loudly with 'expected count sentence not found', so the checker's anchors are updated consciously in the same commit rather than silently skipping a surface.
